newsitem.title: SWEDEN: POLL-Swedish-Bund spread seen wider short-term.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Swedish-Bund spread seen wider short-term.

text.p: Swedish debt has traded around its tightest ever levels over Bunds this week, but a Reuters poll suggests that operators seeking to buy the spread in the short-term will find supply plentiful.

A poll of 10 economists this week found just two bullish short-term expectations for the Sweden-Germany spread, which on Wednesday shrank to 88 basis points, four basis points above a historic low of 84 hit in January.
It had widened slightly and was steady at 90 by Friday.
Longer term, eight out of 10 economists saw the spread breaking below current levels by late 1998, and the median of forecasts had it at 75 basis points by June 1999.

"I wouldn't be surprised if we got a break of 85 in the next few weeks," said Hans Guenter at Chase Manhattan Bank in London. He cited solid economic fundamentals, and scope for economic and monetary union woes to lend Sweden safe-haven attraction.

But most were more cautious near-term: a majority predicted a correction of Sweden's recent strong performance. The mean level for end-1997 was 105 basis points, still down from around 130 this time last year and about 400 in mid-1995.
"Where we are at the moment is not sustainable," said one Swedish-based economist, requesting anonymity. "I think the spread will increase to about 100 basis points quite soon."

Looking further ahead, the range of forecasts was very wide -- from 150 basis points to 30 for June 1999 -- and some economists in the poll described their predictions that far out as plucked out of the air.
A few saw significant economic and monetary union (EMU) convergence trades as a factor around that date.
At Morgan Stanley, Beshara Mahdi was bullish further out, seeing a slight widening in the fourth quarter of this year before the spread inexorably shrinks on convergence trades.
"I strongly believe that public opinion will shift over the next year in favour of EMU membership," he said. "Economic conditions are going to improve and be felt by the average household."
Domestic politics -- Swedes have a general election in autumn 1998 -- were seen by a few economists as likely to gap out the spread around the time of the vote.

"There is a very large risk that higher unemployment will prompt further measures to boost the labour market," said PaineWebber economist James Mackay, envisaging the most dramatic widening of respondents in Q3 1998.

A Swedish-based economist said he expected a new government under pressure from a welfare-hungry population to follow a similar line as recently in Britain, taking a slightly loose fiscal line which would lead to monetary tightening.

But most felt no new government in Sweden was likely to violate recent commitments to get the current account in balance, and eventually into surplus: that would be reflected by a steady shrinkage in the spread.
However at Paribas in London, Ken Wattret saw a directional spread widening, based not so much on Swedish factors as on a view that bund yields would start rising by year-end.

"We're not talking about a disaster, we're just thinking where the risks are skewed from here," he said, echoing comments shared by others that a correction must come eventually after U.S. and German yields ratcheted up so sharply.
